readings.c1s1:
the quantity of any given constituent present in a compound by observing the quantity of a liquid of known strength (called a ''standard solution'') necessary to convert the constituent into another form, the close of the reaction being marked by some definite phenomenon, usually a change of color or the formation of a precipitate. Also called ''volumetric analysis.'' '''ti-tree''' (tē′trē), ''n.'' '''1.''' A palm-lily: same as ''til''1. —'''2.''' Same as ''tea-tree.'' '''tit-tat-to''' (tit′tat-tö′), ''n.'' [< ''tit, tat, to,'' three meaningless syllables used in counting.] A game: same as ''crisscross'', 3. '''titte†''', ''adv.'' See ''tite''1. '''titter1''' (tit′ėr), ''v. i.'' [< ME. ''titeren'', < Icel. ''titra'' = OHG. ''zitterōn'', MHG. ''zitern'', G. ''zittern'', tremble, quiver. Cf. ''teeter, totter''1.] '''1†.''' To move back and forth; sway; waver. {{smaller block|In ''titerynge'' and pursuyte and delayes,
The folk devyne at wagging of a stree. {{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, ii. 1744.}}}} '''2.''' To teeter; seesaw.—'''3.''' To tremble. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.] '''titter2''' (tit′ėr), ''v. i.'' [< ME. *''titeren'' (in deriv. ''titerere'', a tattler), prob. imitative; in part perhaps due to ''titter''1.] To laugh in a restrained or nervous manner, as from suppressed mirth, pleasure, or embarrassment; giggle; snicker. {{smaller block|Thus Sal, with tears in either eye;
While victor Ned sat ''tittering'' by. {{right|''Shenstone'', To a Friend.}} Amy and Louisa Eshton ''tittered'' under their breath. {{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Jane Eyre, xviii.}}}} '''titter2''' (tit′ėr), ''n.'' [< ''titter''2, ''v.''] A restrained
readings.c1s2:
or nervous laugh; a giggle; a snicker.

{{smaller block|There's a ''titter'' of winds in that beechen tree.
{{right|''Bryant'', Gladness of Nature.}}}}

{{smaller block|A strangled ''titter'', out of which there brake
On all sides, clamouring etiquette to death,
Unmeasured mirth.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, v.}}}}

'''titter'''<sup>3</sup> (tit′ėr), ''n.'' [Origin obscure.] A weed, probably the hairy vetch. See ''tine''<sup>3</sup>.

{{smaller block|From wheat go and rake out the ''titters'' or tine.
{{right|''Tusser'', May's Husbandry, st. 19.}}}}

'''titteration''' (tit-e-rā′shon), ''n.'' [< ''titter''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ation''.] A fit of tittering or giggling. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|My brother's arrival has tuned every string of my heart to joy. The holding up of a straw will throw me into a ''titteration''.
{{right|''Richardson'', Sir Charles Grandison, III. lxxi.}}}}

'''titterel''' (tit′ėr-el), ''n.'' [< ''tit''<sup>2</sup> + dim. ''-er-el'' as in ''cockerel'', ''pickerel''.] The whimbrel, ''Numenius phæopus''. [Prov. Eng.]

'''titterer''' (tit′ėr-ėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''titerere'', a tattler: see ''titter''<sup>2</sup>.] 1. One who titters; one who is habitually tittering.

{{smaller block|But he was too short-sighted to notice those who tittered at him—too absent from the world of small facts and petty impulses in which ''titterers'' live.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, iv.}}}}

2†. A tattler.

{{smaller block|Taletellers and ''tyterers''.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xx. 297.}}}}

'''titter-totter''' (tit′ėr-tot″ėr), ''v. i.'' [Formerly also ''tetter-totter''; < ''titter''<sup>1</sup> + ''totter''<sup>1</sup>.] To seesaw; teeter. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''titter-totter''' (tit′ėr-tot″ėr), ''n.'' [< ''titter-totter'', ''v.''] The game of seesaw. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]
readings.c1s3:
¶

'''titter-totter''' (tit′ėr-tot′ėr), ''adv.'' [An elliptical use of ''titter-totter'', ''v.''] In a swaying manner; unsteadily: as, don't stand ''titter-totter''. ''Bailey'', tr. of Colloquies of Erasmus, p. 35.

'''tittery†''', ''n.'' See ''tityre''.

'''tittery-tu†''', ''n.'' See ''tityre-tu''.

'''tittimouse†''', ''n.'' A titmouse.

{{smaller block|The ringdove, redbreast, and the ''tittimouse''.
{{right|''John Taylor'', Works (1630).}}}}

'''tittivate''', ''v.'' See ''titivate''.

'''tittle<sup>1</sup>''' (tit′l), ''v. i.''; pret. and pp. ''tittled'', ppr. ''tittling''. [< ME. *''titelen'' (in deriv. ''titelere'', ''titulere'', a tattler); cf. ''titter''<sup>2</sup>, ''tattle''.] To prate idly; whisper. [Scotch.]

{{smaller block|Here sits a raw [row] of ''tittlin''' jauds.
{{right|''Burns'', Holy Fair.}}}}

'''tittle<sup>2</sup>''' (tit′l), ''n.'' [< ME. ''title'', ''titel'', ''titil'', a title, stroke over a word, etc.; the same as ''title'': see ''title''.] 1. A stroke over a word or letter to show abbreviation; a dot over a letter, as in ''i''. Compare ''iota'' and ''jot''<sup>1</sup>. See ''tilde'', a Spanish form of the same word.

{{smaller block|I'll quote him to a ''tittle''.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Woman-Hater, iii. 2.}}}}

2. A very small thing; a minute object or quantity; a particle; a whit. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|How small the biggest Parts of Earth's proud ''Tittle'' show!
{{right|''Cowley'', Pindaric Odes, x. 1.}}
One jot or one ''tittle'' shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled.
{{right|Mat. v. 18.}}
Right, right; . . . my taste to a ''tittle''.
{{right|''Sheridan'', St. Patrick's Day, i. 1.}}}}
readings.c2s3:
{{smaller block|Had held the bridle, walked his managed mule,
Without a ''tittup'', the procession through.
{{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, I. 212.}}}}

'''tittuppy, tituppy''' (tit′up-i), ''a.'' [< ''tittup'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] 1. Gay; lively; prancing; high-stepping.—2. Shaky; unsteady; ticklish.

{{smaller block|Did you ever see such a little ''tittuppy'' thing in your life? There is not a sound piece of iron about it.
{{right|''Jane Austen'', Northanger Abbey, ix.}}}}

'''titty'''<sup>1</sup> (tit′i), ''n.''; pl. ''titties'' (-iz). [Dim. of ''tit''<sup>1</sup>.] A teat; the breast; especially, the mother's breast: an infantile term.

'''titty'''<sup>2</sup> (tit′i), ''n.'' Sister: an infantile manner of pronouncing the word. ''Burns'', Tam Glen. [Prov. Eng. and Scotch.]

'''titty'''<sup>3</sup> (tit′i), ''n.'' [E. Ind.] An East Indian bagpipe. ''Stainer and Barrett.''

'''tittyrie†''', ''n.'' Same as ''tityre'', 1, for ''tityre-tu.''

'''titty-todger''' (tit′i-toj″ėr), ''n.'' [Cf. ''tiddy''<sup>2</sup>, ''tidy''<sup>2</sup>.] The wren, ''Troglodytes parvulus.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''titubant''' (tit′ū-bant), ''a.'' [= F. ''titubant'' = Sp. ''titubeante'' = Pg. ''titubante, titubeante'', < L. ''tituban(t-)s'', ppr. of ''titubare'', stagger: see ''titubate.''] Staggering; tottering; stumbling. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|Sir Oran's mode of progression being very vacillating, indirect, and ''titubant.'' {{right|''T. L. Peacock'', Melincourt, v.}}}}

'''titubate''' (tit′ụ̄-bāt), ''v. i.''; pret. and pp. ''titubated'', ppr. ''titubating.'' [< L. ''titubatus'', pp. of ''titubare'' (> It. ''titubare'' = Sp. ''titubear'' = Pg. ''titubar, titubear'' = F. ''tituber''), stagger, totter.] To stumble; trip; stagger; reel; rock or roll. [Rare.]

[Corrupt. for ''stickleback''.] Same as ''stickleback''. {{smaller block|There sat the man who had . . . agitated the scientific world with the Theory of ''Tittlebats''. {{right|''Dickens'', Pickwick, i.}}}} '''tittler†''' (tit′lėr), ''n.'' [ME. ''titeler'', ''tuteler'', ''totiler''; < ''tittle''1 + ''-er''1.] A tattler; a prater. {{smaller block|''Tituleris'' . . .
That bablid ffor the best.{{right|''Richard the Redeless'', iv. 57.}} Be no ''totiler''.{{right|''MS. Bibl. Reg.'' 17 B. xvii. f. 141. (''Halliwell''.)}}}} '''tittle-tattle''' (tit′l-tat″l), ''v. i.'' [< ''tittle''1 + ''tattle''; or a varied reduplication of ''tattle''.] To talk idly; prate; gabble. {{smaller block|You must be ''tittle-tattling'' before all our guests.{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., iv. 4. 248.}}}} '''tittle-tattle''' (tit′l-tat″l), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [Early mod. E. also ''title-tatle''; < ''tittle-tattle'', ''v.''] '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' Idle, trifling talk; insignificant gossip. {{smaller block|The daily ''tittle-tattle'' of a court,
By common fame retail'd as office news
In coffee-houses, taverns, cellars, stews.{{right|''Chatterton'', Resignation.}} A readable Life of Pitt, which would give all the facts and none of the ''tittle-tattle'', . . . is quite possible.{{right|''The Academy'', Oct. 18, 1890, p. 336.}}}} '''2.''' An idle, trifling talker; a gossip. [Rare.] {{smaller block|Dame Polupragma, gossip ''Title-tatle'',
Suffers her tongue, let loose at randome, pratle
Of all occurrentes.{{right|''Times' Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 103.}} Impertinent ''Tittletattles'', who have no other variety in their discourse but that of talking slower or faster.{{right|''Addison'', Tatler, No. 157.}}}} '''II.''' ''a.'' Gossiping; gabbling. [Rare.] {{smaller block|And then at christenings and gossips feasts A woman is not seene, the men doe all The ''tittle-tattle'' duties. ''Brome'', Antipodes, i. 6.}} {{smaller block|The ''tittle-tattle'' town. {{right|''W. Combe'', Dr. Syntax's Tours, ii. 31.}}}} '''tittle-tattler''' (tit′l-tat″lėr), ''n.'' One who circulates idle gossip; a trifling tattler. [Rare.] {{smaller block|It was somewhat doubtful whether the ''tittle-tatler'' had improved on the usual version of the story. {{right|''The Academy'', Jan. 29, 1889, p. 76.}}}} '''tittle-tattling''' (tit′l-tat″ling), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''tittle-tattle'', ''v.''] The practice of dealing in idle gossip; a tattling about trifles. {{smaller block|You are full in your ''tittle-tattlings'' of Cupid; here is Cupid, and there is Cupid. ''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, ii.}} '''tittup, titup''' (tit′up), ''v. i.'' [< ''tit'', appar. a vague variant of ''tip''2, + ''up''.] To act or go in a gay, lively, or impatient manner; spring; prance; skip. {{smaller block|It would be endless to notice . . . the "Dear me's" and "Oh la's" of the ''titupping'' misses. {{right|''Scott'', St. Ronan's Well, xiii.}}}} {{smaller block|A magnificent horse dancing, and ''tittupping'', and tossing, and performing the most graceful caracoles and gambadoes. ''Thackeray'', Philip, viii.}} '''tittup, titup''' (tit′up), ''n.'' [< ''tittup'', ''v.''] A lively or gay movement or gait; a prancing or springing about; a canter. {{smaller block|Citizens in Crowds, upon Pads, Hackneys, and Hunters; all upon the ''Tittup'', as if he who Rid not a Gallop was to forfeit his Horse. {{right|Quoted in ''Ashton's'' Social Life in Reign of Queen Anne, [I. 84.}} Had held the bridle, walked his managed mule, Without a ''tittup'', the procession through. {{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, I. 212.}}}} '''tittuppy, tituppy''' (tit′up-i), ''a.'' [< ''tittup'' + ''-y''1.] 1. Gay; lively; prancing; high-stepping.—2. Shaky; unsteady; ticklish. {{smaller block|Did you ever see such a little ''tittuppy'' thing in your life? There is not a sound piece of iron about it. {{right|''Jane Austen'', Northanger Abbey, ix.}}}} '''titty'''1 (tit′i), ''n.''; pl. ''titties'' (-iz). [Dim. of ''tit''1.] A teat; the breast; especially, the mother's breast: an infantile term. '''titty'''2 (tit′i), ''n.'' Sister: an infantile manner of pronouncing the word. ''Burns'', Tam Glen. [Prov. Eng. and Scotch.] '''titty'''3 (tit′i), ''n.'' [E. Ind.] An East Indian bagpipe. ''Stainer and Barrett.'' '''tittyrie†''', ''n.'' Same as ''tityre'', 1, for ''tityre-tu.'' '''titty-todger''' (tit′i-toj″ėr), ''n.'' [Cf. ''tiddy''2, ''tidy''2.] The wren, ''Troglodytes parvulus.'' [Prov. Eng.] '''titubant''' (tit′ū-bant), ''a.'' [= F. ''titubant'' = Sp. ''titubeante'' = Pg. ''titubante, titubeante'', < L. ''tituban(t-)s'', ppr. of ''titubare'', stagger: see ''titubate.''] Staggering; tottering; stumbling. [Rare.] {{smaller block|Sir Oran's mode of progression being very vacillating, indirect, and ''titubant.'' {{right|''T. L. Peacock'', Melincourt, v.}}}} '''titubate''' (tit′ụ̄-bāt), ''v. i.''; pret. and pp. ''titubated'', ppr. ''titubating.'' [< L. ''titubatus'', pp. of ''titubare'' (> It. ''titubare'' = Sp. ''titubear'' = Pg. ''titubar, titubear'' = F. ''tituber''), stagger, totter.] To stumble; trip; stagger; reel; rock or roll. [Rare.] {{smaller block|But what became of this ''titubating'', this towering mountain of snow? {{right|''Waterhouse'', Apol. for Learning, p. 29. (''Latham.'')}}}} '''titubation''' (tit-ū-bā′shọn), ''n.'' [= F. ''titubation'' = Pg. ''titubeação'' = It. ''titubazione'', < L. ''titubatio(n-)'', a staggering, < ''titubare'', stagger: see ''titubate''.] 1. The act of stumbling or staggering; a tottering.—2. In ''med.'', restlessness; an inclination to constant change of position; fidgets.—3. The act of rocking or rolling, as a curved body on a plane. '''titular''' (tit′ū-lär), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [= F. ''titulaire'' = Sp. Pg. ''titular'' = It. ''titolare'', < ML. *''titularis'', pertaining to a title, < L. ''titulus'', title: see ''title''.] I. ''a.'' 1. Of, pertaining to, or having a title, in any sense; existing in or by reason of title; so designated or entitled: as, ''titular'' rank, dignity, or rights; ''titular'' possession; a ''titular'' professor or incumbent of office (that is, one bearing the title, in distinction from an adjunct or a deputy). {{smaller block|The ''titular'' Dr. Lamb is committed to the Gate-house, about causing a Westminster scholar to give himself to the devil. {{right|''Court and Times of Charles I.'', I. 305.}}}} 2. Existing in or having the title only; being such only in name; so-called; nominal; not actual: as, a ''titular'' sovereignty or bishopric; the line of ''titular'' kings of Jerusalem. {{smaller block|I appeal to any Reader if this is not the Conditions in which these ''Titular'' Odes appear. {{right|''Congreve'', On the Pindaric Ode.}}}} {{smaller block|This ''titular'' sovereign of half a dozen empires, in which he did not actually possess a rood of land. {{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., i. 2.}}}} 3. Receiving the name (of), or used by name, as part of a title; giving or taking title. See quotation, and ''titular church'', below. {{smaller block|The present cardinals ''titular'' of the basilican churches of San Marco, and of the Sti. Apostoli. {{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., VI. 207.}}}} {{smaller|'''Titular abbot.''' See ''abbot.''—'''Titular bishop''', in the ''Rom. Cath. Ch.'', a bishop bearing the name of a former Christian see in which the Christian church has ceased to exist, chiefly in Mohammedan countries. This term was substituted by decree of the Propaganda, 1882, for that of "bishop in partibus infidelium," formerly in use. A titular bishop is usually assigned to episcopal duties in a country or locality where no Roman Catholic diocese exists or can be established, under the local designation of ''vicar apostolic.''—'''Titular church''', one of the parish churches of Rome, the names of which are used in the titles of cardinal priests. Compare ''title'', ''n.'', 15 (''a'').}} '''II.''' ''n.'' 1. A person who holds a title of office, or a right of possession independently of the functions or obligations properly implied by it; in ''eccles. law'', one who may lawfully enjoy a benefice without performing its duties.—2. One whose name is used as a title; specifically, the patron saint of a church.—{{smaller|'''Titular of a church''', in the ''Rom. Cath. Ch.'', that sacred person or thing from which a church receives its title: the term is wider than ''patron'', and may comprehend the persons of the Trinity, the mysteries, or the saints, while a patron can be only a saint or an angel. ''Cath. Dict.''—'''Titulars of the tithes''', in ''Scotch eccles. law'', the titulars or lay patrons to whom the teinds or tenth part of the produce of lands, formerly claimed by the clergy, had been granted by the crown.}} '''titularity''' (tit-ụ̄-lar′i-ti), ''n.'' [< ''titular'' + ''-it-y''.] The state of being titular; use as a title of office. {{smaller block|Julius, Augustus, and Tiberius with great humility or popularity refused the name of Imperator, but their successors have challenged that title, and retained the same even in its ''titularity''. {{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Vulg. Err., vii. 16.}}}} '''titularly''' (tit′ū-lär-li), ''adv.'' In a titular manner; by or with regard to title; nominally. '''titulary''' (tit′ū-lā-ri), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [= F. ''titulaire'' = It. ''titolario'', < ML. *''titularius'', pertaining to a title (cf. ''titularius'', n., a writer of titles), < L. ''titulus'', a title: see ''title'', and cf. ''titular''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Consisting in a title; bearing a title; titular. {{smaller block|Richard Smith, ''titulary'' Bishop of Chalcedon, taking his honour from Greece, his profit from England (where he bishoped it over all the Romish Catholics), was now very busy. {{right|''Fuller'', Ch. Hist., XI. ii. 7.}}}} '''2.''' Of or pertaining to a title; dependent upon or proceeding from a right or title. {{smaller block|William . . . the Conquerour, howsoever he used and exercised the power of a Conquerour to reward his Normans, yet . . . mixed it with a ''Titulary'' pretence grounded upon the will and designation of Edward the Confessor. {{right|''Bacon'', Hist. Henry VII., p. 5.}}}} '''II.''' ''n.''; pl. ''titularies'' (-riz). The holder of a title; a titular incumbent or holder. {{smaller block|The persons deputed for the celebration of these masses were neither ''titularies'' nor perpetual curates, but persons entirely conductitious. {{right|''Ayliffe'', Parergon.}}}} '''tituled†''' (tit′ūld), ''a.'' [< L. ''titulus'', title (see ''title''), + ''-ed''2.] Having or bearing a title; entitled. '''titup, tituppy.''' See ''tittup, tittuppy''. '''tit-warbler''' (tit′wâr″blėr), ''n.'' A bird of the subfamily ''Parinæ''. ''Swainson.''
